A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Virtual Community and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Renumbered sections and relocated appendix material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original assistance, social-influence, robot-cooperation and commute experiments, together with scene-quality and simulation-speed benchmarks.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds component ablations, VLA evaluation and memory-scaling measurements.

M1.justification: The proposed scene-generation, community-generation and Genesis simulation procedures remain substantively unchanged. The initialization reachability check and robot-training details are newly documented, without establishing a procedural revision. VLA and decomposed RL are additional benchmark implementations and ablation variants.

E1.justification: The generated scene collection and assistance, influence, robot and commute task coverage are retained. Robot delivery already appeared in v1 Table 2 despite its narrower task description. The additional training trajectories and experiments concern existing task coverage.

E2.justification: The robot comparison expands beyond heuristic and oracle-grasp PPO variants to include PPO without oracle grasp and a fine-tuned pi0 VLA baseline with oracle grasp (v2 Tables 4 and 11). Mixed GPT-4o/o1 social agents and decomposed RL also broaden the evaluated comparison configurations.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark scene counts, task metrics and principal evaluation settings are retained. Added experiments introduce controlled component substitutions, a memory-measurement protocol spanning 1–50 agents on an L40S, and VLA-specific fine-tuning, 224×224 observations and 20 Hz control. These supplement the existing protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds distance-modeling ablations for MCTS and LLM planners, a target-selection versus dialogue-backbone ablation, and separate reach/place RL policies (Tables 2, 3 and 5). Appendix E.2 additionally tests memory scaling with agent count. The advanced-task analysis already present in v1 is retained.

E5.justification: The existing KID uncertainty values remain unchanged in v1 Table 5 and v2 Table 8. Neither version supplies seed or repeated-run counts for the task benchmarks, and the added experiments introduce no confidence intervals, significance tests or new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises MCTS human-following rates from 0.0 to 7.7 and 8.0 for one and two assistants, and the two-assistant LLM rate from 7.6 to 10.7. New results include robot average SRs of 14.3 for non-oracle RL and 2.4 for oracle-grasp VLA, component-ablation outcomes and memory-scaling measurements. Existing scene-quality, advanced-planning and commute scores are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix F.5 adds an explicit mathematical definition of the robot reward using clamped distance penalties and grasp/placement bonuses, absent from v1's brief PPO description. Existing commute-planning equations are unchanged, and no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a unified human–robot simulation platform, scalable geospatially grounded world/community generation, and two principal multi-agent challenges. The abstract is condensed, but the main scientific contributions and conclusion retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds focused interpretations of distance dependence, cooperation compensating for missing spatial information, dialogue versus target-selection contributions, and VLA failure from task/domain gaps and limited fine-tuning. It also interprets memory growth as approximately linear. The visual-fidelity and agent-capacity limitations already appeared in v1 Appendix L and move to v2 J.3.

D1.justification: Appendices F.5–F.6 substantially expand robot reproducibility information through reward specifications, PPO architecture and hyperparameters, and VLA trajectory collection, preprocessing, inputs and training settings. v2 also documents initialization reachability checks, GUI shortcuts and data-handling practices. The earlier 2 m/s avatar walking-speed disclosure is omitted.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to pi0 (Black et al., 2024a) and RSL-RL (Schwarke et al., 2025) for the new baseline and implementation documentation. The broader positioning relative to simulation platforms, embodied social intelligence and generative environments remains essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected methodological paragraphs are condensed or clarified. Unified simulation moves from Section 4 to Section 3.3, avatar subsections are merged, and appendix discussion, resources and limitations are reorganized. Affiliations and publication headers change, while most prose and prompt content remain closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 adds three ablation tables, RL-configuration and VLA-result tables, a keyboard-shortcut table, a memory plot and a GUI screenshot. The robot table is regrouped by oracle-grasp availability, existing displays are relocated, and the document is comprehensively reformatted into the ICLR layout. Most existing illustrations and plots are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the benchmarks more informative and reproducible through component controls, a VLA comparison, memory measurements and explicit robot-training specifications. These gains are tempered by continued point-estimate reporting and an overbroad social-ablation interpretation: Table 3 shows that o1 target selection increases friendship wins while reducing conversion rates. The net improvement is useful but limited.
